title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHAT YOU THINK
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHAT YOU THINK
Before you throw away the tree—or defend it—there is a harder question every Christian needs to answer: What does Jesus actually want from you?
Every December, it happens again.
One Christian posts a picture of a Christmas tree glowing beside a Bible.
Another Christian comments, “That’s pagan.”
Someone replies, “We’re celebrating Jesus.”
Someone else says, “Jesus wasn’t born on December 25.”
Then Jeremiah 10 gets quoted.
Romans 14 gets quoted back.
Voices rise.
Defenses go up.
Brothers and sisters who both claim the name of Christ begin treating each other like enemies over lights, trees, calendars, gifts, traditions, and a date the Bible itself never gives us.
And somewhere in the middle of all the noise...
Jesus can become almost invisible.
That may be the most uncomfortable Christmas problem of all.
Because perhaps the deepest question is not simply, “Should Christians celebrate Christmas?”
Perhaps the question underneath the question is:
Can I do what I am doing with a clear conscience before Jesus Christ—and is what I am doing actually bringing glory to Him?
That question cuts deeper.
Because you can put up a Christmas tree and forget Christ.
You can also throw away your Christmas tree and become proud of how much more “biblical” you think you are than everyone else.
You can sing about Bethlehem while refusing to forgive someone.
You can condemn December 25 while carrying bitterness in your heart.
You can buy gifts for everyone you love while ignoring the Savior who gave Himself for you.
And you can know every argument about Saturnalia, Roman festivals, calendars, shepherds, trees, and church history...
while your own heart remains miles from Jesus.
So before deciding whether Christmas belongs in your home, we need to go somewhere much older than Christmas.
Back before December 25.
Back before church calendars.
Back before decorated trees.
Back before Christmas carols.
Back to a frightened young mother.
A manger.
A dark night.
Shepherds watching their flocks.
And an announcement that shook eternity.
Luke records the angel declaring that good news had arrived because a Savior had been born, identified as Christ the Lord.
The center of the announcement was not a date.
It was a Person.
Jesus.
And John reaches even deeper into the mystery of that arrival:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
John 1:14.
Those Greek words are staggering.
ὁ Λόγος — ho Logos — the Word.
σὰρξ — sarx — flesh.
ἐγένετο — egeneto — became.
The eternal Word entered human existence.
God did not merely send humanity another philosophy.
He came near.
The Son took flesh.
John continues:
καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν
kai eskēnōsen en hēmin
“and dwelt among us.”
The verb eskēnōsen carries the imagery of dwelling or pitching one’s tent among a people.
Think about that.
The Christmas story, stripped of commercialism and sentimentality, is not fundamentally about snow, presents, trees, family dinners, nostalgia, or December 25.
It is about the incomprehensible humility of Christ.
The Creator entered His creation.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world of human hunger, exhaustion, rejection, suffering, betrayal, blood, nails, and death.
Bethlehem was already pointing toward Calvary.
The Child in the manger came to become the Lamb on the cross.
That is Christianity.
And that is where our Christmas question must begin.
Not with, “What does my family normally do?”
Not with, “What does social media say?”
Not even with, “What did Christians hundreds of years ago do?”
But with Scripture.
And Scripture gives us something that frustrates people on both extremes.
The Bible does not command Christians to celebrate the birth of Jesus annually on December 25.
But neither does the New Testament issue a command forbidding Christians from setting aside a day to remember and give thanks for Christ's incarnation.
That matters.
December 25 is not identified in Scripture as Jesus' birthday. Christians therefore should not pretend the Bible tells us the exact date when Christ was born.
It doesn't.

Historical discussion about why December 25 eventually became associated with the celebration of Christ's birth is more complicated than the popular slogan “Christians simply stole a pagan holiday.” Various historical explanations have been proposed, and Christians should be careful about repeating sweeping claims as unquestionable facts when the history is debated.
But even after studying all of that history, we still have to answer the more important theological question.
What should a Christian do now?
Paul gives us a remarkably relevant principle in Romans 14.
The Greek text of Romans 14:5 reads:
ὃς μὲν γὰρ κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ’ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν· ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω.
Hos men gar krinei hēmeran par’ hēmeran, hos de krinei pasan hēmeran; hekastos en tō idiō noi plērophoreisthō.

In context, Paul describes one believer regarding one day differently from another while another regards the days alike, and then says that each should be fully persuaded or convinced in his own mind.
The passage is not specifically about modern Christmas.
We should not pretend that it is.
But its principle concerning disputed observances of days is enormously important.
Paul continues by bringing the issue underneath one governing reality:
“to the Lord.”
The person observing a day must observe it to the Lord.
That changes everything.
The question becomes painfully personal.
When you celebrate Christmas...
is it actually to the Lord?
Not to nostalgia.
Not to consumerism.
Not because everyone else is doing it.
Not because you are terrified of disappointing relatives.
Not because you want impressive family photographs.
Not because your children need more things.
Not because December would feel strange without the traditions.
To the Lord.
And for the Christian who chooses not to celebrate Christmas, the question is equally uncomfortable.
Are you abstaining to the Lord?
Or have you quietly begun to enjoy feeling spiritually superior to Christians who celebrate it?
Because Romans 14 does not merely address liberty.
It attacks contempt.
It attacks judgmentalism.
The Christian who celebrates must not despise the Christian who abstains.
The Christian who abstains must not condemn a brother or sister merely because that believer, in sincere conscience, dedicates a day to remembering Christ's incarnation.
There are boundaries, of course.
Christian liberty does not turn idolatry into worship.
Calling something “Christian” cannot sanctify sin.
If a celebration requires drunkenness, sexual immorality, greed, occult practices, idolatry, dishonesty, or anything else Scripture condemns, attaching Jesus' name to it does not make it holy.
Paul gives another governing principle:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.”
That principle from 1 Corinthians 10:31 reaches straight into December.
Can Christ be glorified in your celebration?
Can you thank Him for taking flesh?
Can you open Scripture with your children and tell them why Bethlehem matters?
Can you feed someone who is hungry?
Can you reconcile with someone you have wounded?
Can you give without worshiping possessions?
Can you remember the lonely?
Can you invite the forgotten person to your table?
Can you tell an unbelieving relative why Jesus came?
Can your home say something more powerful than “Merry Christmas”?
Can your life say:
Christ has come. Christ has died. Christ is risen. Christ saves sinners.
Then there is another argument that appears every year.
“The Christmas tree is condemned in Jeremiah 10.”
Read the chapter carefully.
Jeremiah is confronting idolatry. The passage describes craftsmen working material into an idol and adorning it, within a larger contrast between powerless idols and the living God.
It is not a prophecy about a modern family placing a decorated evergreen in a living room.
That does not mean Christians should never examine their traditions.
We absolutely should.
Anything can become an idol.
A tree can.
Money can.
Family can.
Tradition can.
Even theological knowledge can.
But biblical interpretation requires us to ask what a passage meant in its actual context before making it address a practice centuries removed from that context.
Ironically, a Christian could have no Christmas tree at all and still be drowning in idolatry.
Because idols are not limited to objects carved from wood.
Sometimes an idol looks like success.
Sometimes it looks like approval.
Sometimes it looks like money.
Sometimes it looks like romance.
Sometimes it looks like ministry.
Sometimes it even looks like being right.
And suddenly the Christmas debate becomes uncomfortable again.
Because maybe Jesus is not asking first about the tree standing in your living room.
Maybe He is confronting what is sitting on the throne of your heart.
Imagine celebrating the birth of Jesus while refusing His lordship.
Imagine singing:
“Christ the Savior is born,”
while secretly cherishing the sin from which the Savior came to rescue you.
Imagine defending the manger while rejecting the cross.
That is the real tragedy.
Jesus did not enter this world merely so humanity could create a beautiful holiday around His infancy.
He came to save sinners.
The manger cannot be separated from the cross.
Matthew tells us why His name would be Jesus: He would save His people from their sins.
Not decorate their sins.
Not excuse their sins.
Not rename their sins.
Save them.
Christmas without repentance can become sentimental Christianity.
A baby Jesus who never grows up is very easy for the world to tolerate.
A baby in a manger makes a beautiful decoration.
But the Jesus who grows up and says, “Follow Me”...
the Jesus who confronts hypocrisy...
the Jesus who commands repentance...
the Jesus who identifies Himself as the way, the truth, and the life...
the Jesus who willingly goes to the cross...
the Jesus who rises from the grave...
the Jesus before whom every knee will ultimately bow...
that Jesus cannot simply be placed back into a storage box when December ends.
And perhaps that is the Christmas question we have been avoiding.
Not:
“Do you celebrate Christmas?”
But:
Does Christ have you?
Because you can celebrate Christmas and belong to Jesus.
You can abstain from Christmas and belong to Jesus.
But you cannot belong to Jesus while deliberately refusing Jesus Himself.
Maybe you are reading this with Christmas memories that hurt.
Perhaps December does not feel magical to you.
Maybe there is an empty chair at your table now.
Someone died.
Someone left.
Someone betrayed you.
Maybe the family photograph changed.
Maybe the marriage ended.
Maybe your child no longer calls.
Maybe you are surrounded by Christmas lights while fighting a darkness nobody around you can see.
Everyone keeps saying, “Merry Christmas.”
And you keep smiling.
But something inside you whispers:
“I just want this month to be over.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel was never dependent upon your circumstances being merry.
Jesus entered a broken world.
He came into political tension, poverty, danger, grief, violence, and eventually exile.
The Christmas story itself contains tears.
And Christ did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up enough for God.
He came because we could not save ourselves.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace for the addict who relapsed.
Grace for the religious person hiding pride.
Grace for the husband who failed.
Grace for the wife who feels invisible.
Grace for the prodigal who thinks he has traveled too far.
Grace for the churchgoer who sings loudly but secretly wonders whether God still wants him.
Grace for the woman crying after everyone has gone to sleep.
Grace for the man who keeps telling everyone he is fine.
Grace for you.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that good people finally managed to climb high enough to reach God.
It is that God came down for sinners.
ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
The Word became flesh.
He came down.
And eventually...
He was lifted up on a cross.
There the hands that Mary once held were pierced.
The forehead she once kissed was wounded.
The body once wrapped in swaddling cloth was stripped and crucified.
And the One whose birth angels announced died beneath the judgment our sins deserved.
Then the grave received Him.
For three days, it appeared that darkness had won.
But Christianity does not end at a manger.
And it does not end at a cross.
The tomb became empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why grace can rewrite your story.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your betrayal does not get the last word.
Your grief does not get the last word.
Your past does not get the last word.
Death itself does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
That is what we mean when we say:
So...
should Christians celebrate Christmas?
A Christian should not pretend that Scripture commands an annual December 25 celebration when it does not.
A Christian should not condemn another believer merely for sincerely setting aside a day to remember Christ's incarnation when Scripture does not issue such a prohibition.
A Christian who celebrates should do so under the lordship of Christ, with thanksgiving and a clear conscience.
A Christian who abstains should abstain under the lordship of Christ, with thanksgiving and a clear conscience.
Neither side should turn a matter of conscience into a throne from which to look down upon the other.
And every Christian should be willing to examine traditions in the light of Scripture.
If Christmas in your home has become greed...
change it.
If it has become drunkenness...
repent.
If it has become debt-fueled competition...
change it.
If it has become an exhausting performance designed to impress people...
change it.
If Santa receives more attention than Jesus...
ask yourself why.
If your children know every detail of a fictional Christmas story but barely understand why the Son of God came into the world...
something needs to change.
You do not necessarily need to throw Christmas away.
You may need to redeem the way you observe it.
Open Luke 2.
Read Matthew 1.
Read John 1.
Tell your children about the incarnation.
Pray together.
Give quietly.
Forgive somebody.
Visit someone lonely.
Feed somebody.
Support Gospel work.
Tell somebody who does not know Christ why the manger matters.
And when the lights eventually come down...
keep following Jesus.
That is the test.
January Jesus.
February Jesus.
March Jesus.
When there are no carols playing.
When the decorations are gone.
When following Him costs something.
When obedience hurts.
When temptation whispers.
When nobody applauds.
Jesus.
Still Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Be honest.
Somebody reading it may desperately need proof that Jesus still restores people.
And perhaps even send it privately to the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious tradition.
Let them discover that Christianity is not ultimately about Christmas.
It is about Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never could.
It doesn't.
Jesus purchased salvation with His blood. Grace cannot be bought.
Christians hold different convictions about tithing, while the New Testament clearly emphasizes willing, purposeful, generous giving rather than giving under compulsion.

If you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior keep producing Christ-centered content, reach hurting people, develop discipleship resources, and expand this work, monthly support is one practical way.
Scripture teaches a beautiful principle of Christian generosity: giving should come from a heart that has decided to give, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That matters to us.
We do not want your support because someone frightened, pressured, or spiritually manipulated you into giving.
We want Jesus to receive the glory.
So pray about it.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Because someone you know is fighting a battle they have never posted about.
Someone is smiling through spiritual exhaustion.
Someone thinks Jesus could never forgive what they have done.
Someone believes their scandal has become their identity.
Someone thinks their story is already over.
Share truth with them.
Share hope with them.
And if this ministry consistently helps you do that, prayerfully consider helping us keep doing it too.
Because after every argument about Christmas eventually fades...
after the tree comes down...
after the gifts break...
after the lights burn out...
after December becomes another memory...
one question remains.
What did you do with Jesus?
Do not merely celebrate the day people remember His birth.
Know Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
Follow Him.
And let the Savior who entered humanity's darkness enter every locked room of your heart.
Because the greatest Christmas miracle is not that humanity finally found its way to God.
It is that, in Jesus Christ...
God came looking for us.
And when Jesus enters the story, even the chapter you were ashamed to show anyone can become the place where grace begins writing again.
